spec.title: The coverage spine: one control, seven stages, a green gate
spec.intro:
This is the capstone's guided portion: the coverage spine. Your surface is a simulated
capstone repo seeded byte-identically to what `bash labs/setup.sh` writes — the manifest,
the seven placeholder stage artifacts, the before/after skeleton — and a "Validate
capstone" button that runs the lab's own `validate-capstone.sh`, ported to engine code and
CI-verified byte-for-byte against real `bash` runs of that script. Every per-stage line,
verdict, and exit code you see here is what the real validator prints on a real machine.

Two honest boundaries. First: the engineering artifacts themselves (your collect script,
your policy, your scheduled workflow) are built in your real environment per Modules 5–13;
here they are the setup script's placeholders, and the work is the manifest-and-validator
loop that proves coverage. Second: in this simulation the validator is engine code — you
literally cannot edit it to make it pass. On your real machine you could, and §6 task 2
names that as the exact anti-pattern this program teaches against.

The control you'll ship is the one this program has carried since week 0: laptop disk
encryption — the same claim you watched a Mac answer with `fdesetup status` and a Windows
box answer with `Get-BitLockerVolume`. The eight-point checklist above the editor is read
from the validator's own output; your job is to make it green, break it in the two ways
real capstones break, read the difference, and make it green again — twice.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 1. The seeded manifest still claims the fixture's S3 control. Re-found it for
the control you are shipping: in the manifest editor, replace the `control:` line with
exactly `control: "Company laptops enforce full-disk encryption (SOC 2 CC6.1)"` —
and leave all seven `loop_coverage:` stage mappings and the `before_after:` pointer in
place. In your real capstone this line names YOUR control and every mapping names a
real artifact; a stage you can't name an artifact for is a gap to close, not a line to
leave implicit.

hints.nudge: Only one line changes. The seven loop_coverage rows and the before_after pointer are the coverage spine — they stay exactly as setup.sh wrote them.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the manifest makes coverage machine-checkable: one stage, one named artifact

hints.reveal: In the editor, replace the control: line with: control: "Company laptops enforce full-disk encryption (SOC 2 CC6.1)" — touch nothing else

tasks.explain:
The capstone now names the claim this whole program has been sixteen ways of checking:
the week-0 laptop-encryption analysis is your "before," and the manifest you just
edited is the spine the "after" hangs on. Notice what did NOT change — the seven
stage-to-artifact rows. The control is yours; the coverage contract is invariant.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 2, first run. Before you click, predict all nine output lines: seven stage
rows, one before/after row, one verdict. Then press "Validate capstone" and reconcile.
Every stage should read `ok` with its artifact named, the verdict line should be the
PASS sentence, and the exit code should be 0 — the same transcript the real validator
prints over this manifest on a real machine.

verify.stdout_matches: ^PASS: all 7 loop stages covered; before/after present$

hints.nudge: The validator prints one aligned row per stage — `ok` names the artifact that discharges it, `MISSING` names the gap. The last line is the verdict; the exit code is the gate.

hints.concept: §5.2 — the verdict line IS the gate: the curriculum eating its own dog food

hints.reveal: Click "Validate capstone": every stage reads ok, the before/after row reads ok, the final line is `PASS: all 7 loop stages covered; before/after present`, exit 0

tasks.explain:
That per-stage transcript is §5.1's coverage table, asserted by a machine instead of
claimed in prose. The column alignment isn't cosmetic — it's the validator's own
printf, and the module's CI greps those exact columns. The exit code is the part a
pipeline consumes: 0 ships, anything else names what doesn't.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 2, the failure it warns about — made real. A capstone that claims coverage it
doesn't have is the §5.4 failure mode, so reproduce it deliberately: in the manifest
editor, delete the entire `MONITOR:` row and the entire `before_after:` line, then
validate. The validator must name BOTH gaps — `no artifact mapped` for MONITOR, the
before/after pointer absent — and exit 1. This is exactly the shape of the committed
`capstone-manifest-incomplete.yaml` fixture the module's own CI replays as its
negative case.

verify.stdout_matches: ^  before/after MISSING \(no before_after pointer or file not found\)$
^FAIL: capstone coverage incomplete — close the named gaps before shipping$

hints.nudge: Two deletions: the MONITOR row inside the loop_coverage block, and the top-level before_after pointer. Then run the gate and read what it names.

hints.concept: §4.1 — a stage with no artifact next to it is a gap, full stop; naming it honestly beats pretending it's covered

hints.reveal: Delete `  MONITOR:    .github/workflows/ccm.yml` and `before_after: before-after.md`, then Validate capstone — MONITOR MISSING (no artifact mapped), before/after MISSING, FAIL, exit 1

tasks.explain:
The gate discriminated: green on full coverage, red with NAMED gaps on partial — that
discrimination is what makes it a control check rather than a ceremony. Exit 1 means a
CI pipeline would refuse to ship this capstone, and the per-stage output tells the
author exactly which artifact to produce next. Do not edit the gate; close the gap.

tasks.instruction:
Now the subtler failure: a manifest can claim an artifact that is not there. Restore
the `before_after: before-after.md` line, and map MONITOR to a workflow that does not
exist — `MONITOR:    .github/workflows/monitor.yml` — then validate. Read the output
carefully: `MISSING (artifact not found: …)` is a different fact from
`MISSING (no artifact mapped)`. The first is a claim the repo contradicts; the second
is a claim never made. Reviewers meet the first kind far more often.

hints.nudge: Mapping a path doesn't make it real — the validator resolves every mapped path against the repo beside the manifest. Two different MISSING messages exist; this task produces the other one.

hints.concept: §4.6 — done is falsifiable: a stage that is claimed is not the same as a stage that is satisfied

hints.reveal: Re-add `before_after: before-after.md`, change the MONITOR row to `  MONITOR:    .github/workflows/monitor.yml`, Validate capstone — MONITOR MISSING (artifact not found: .github/workflows/monitor.yml), before/after ok, exit 1

tasks.explain:
This is §5.4 in miniature: the manifest said MONITOR was covered and the repo said
otherwise — the validator caught the manifest lying, not just staying silent. Both
failures exit 1, but the messages route differently: "no artifact mapped" means decide
and name; "artifact not found" means the named thing must be produced or the claim
withdrawn. Distinguishing them is the diagnosis skill the §7 rubric checks.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 7. Close the gap with the artifact that actually exists: point MONITOR back at
`.github/workflows/ccm.yml` (setup.sh wrote it; only your mapping was wrong), validate,
and confirm all seven stages plus the before/after read ok with exit 0. Then validate a
second time without touching anything: the verdict must be identical — your coverage
proof is itself reproducible.

verify.stdout_matches: ^PASS: all 7 loop stages covered; before/after present$

hints.nudge: The workflow file was in the repo all along — the gap was in your claim, not your artifacts. Re-point the mapping, run the gate, then run it again and compare verdicts.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the manifest maps stages to artifacts; the validator asserts the mapping resolves, every run, identically

hints.reveal: Change the MONITOR row back to `  MONITOR:    .github/workflows/ccm.yml`, click Validate capstone (PASS, exit 0), then click it once more — the transcript is identical

tasks.explain:
Two runs, one verdict: the proof is a pure function of repo state, which is what lets
the module's own happy-path script assert reproducibility by comparing the verdict
line across consecutive runs of the real validator. A coverage proof that drifts
between runs would be exactly the unfalsifiable promise this program exists to retire.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 3, for your control. Draft the `control-statement.md` that discharges
UNDERSTAND and LOCATE for the laptop-encryption claim: the claim in your own words;
the threat it mitigates, cited the Module-11 way (a lost or stolen laptop exposing
data at rest); and the named ground-truth location — specific enough that someone else
could fetch it. For this control that means naming the actual field on the actual
system: what `fdesetup status` reports on a Mac, what the volume protection status of
`Get-BitLockerVolume` reports on Windows. "The MDM says so" is a derived answer, not
ground truth — say where the truth lives.

hints.nudge: Three parts: claim, threat, ground truth. The test of the third: could a colleague who has never met you fetch the value from what you wrote alone?

hints.concept: §5.1 — if you can't name the LOCATE artifact, you don't yet know where the truth lives

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 4, the seam — and the validator's honest limit. Look at what the seeded
placeholders actually do: `collect.sh` emits an empty bucket list, the rego policy is
a stub, and `ccm.yml` declares a schedule but never invokes collect.sh or the policy.
Yet the validator just printed `MONITOR ok` and exited 0. In 3–5 sentences: what does
the validator actually verify (presence of a mapped artifact), what must a reviewer
verify that it cannot (the seam — the scheduled path invoking the SAME
QUERY → EVALUATE → EVIDENCE code as your hand run, and producing the verdict the
evidence records), and write the one-sentence agreement statement §6 task 4 asks you
to put in before-after.md once you have verified the hand-run and scheduled paths
agree in your real environment.

hints.nudge: A scheduled job that collects but never evaluates or alerts is logging wearing monitoring's clothes — §5.4's exact diagnosis. The coverage gate can't see that; the seam check can.

hints.concept: §4.3 — integration is where the seams are, and the scheduled run is the truth

tasks.instruction:
§6 tasks 5 and 6, plus the §7 walkthrough — the product half of shipping. For your
real control, draft: (a) the README product section — the customers who depend on the
control's output, ONE accountable named owner (a person, not a team alias), three
backlog items including at least one honest known gap, the single metric that says
it's working, and one sentence of UX rationale (evidence as a by-product of the work);
(b) the before/after — the same control's week-0 legacy state beside its engineered
state on at least four concrete dimensions (effort, frequency, drift detection,
durability), scored against the five legacy problems, with at least one residual gap
that did NOT improve, cross-referenced to a backlog item from (a); and (c) two or
three sentences you would say to a stakeholder who has never read the manifesto,
arguing from the before/after and the live monitoring — not assertion — why the
engineered control is more trustworthy than its legacy predecessor.

hints.nudge: A before/after that is all upside is not credible; the honest residual gap, cross-referenced to your own backlog, is what makes a reviewer trust the rest.

hints.concept: §4.4 and §4.5 — five named product elements; the before/after is a controlled comparison, not a brag

files.content:
# Sample INCOMPLETE capstone manifest (committed fixture, negative-case).
# MONITOR is missing from loop_coverage and there is no before_after pointer.
# The validator MUST reject this (name the gaps, exit non-zero) — proving the
# coverage gate actually gates, instead of rubber-stamping. This is the §5.4
# "weak capstone" failure mode made machine-detectable.
control: "S3 buckets block public access (SOC 2 CC6.1)"
owner: "a.engineer@example.com"
loop_coverage:
  UNDERSTAND: control-statement.md
  LOCATE:     control-statement.md
  QUERY:      collect.sh
  EVALUATE:   policy/public_access.rego
  EVIDENCE:   evidence/
  OWN:        README.md
